conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. You were admitted for nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’m feeling a bit better since the IV fluids in the ER. Still a little nauseous, but no vomiting today. My stomach burns in the middle, but it gets better after I go to the bathroom.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And the diarrhea—how many times a day? Is it watery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, watery and yellow. I had four episodes the day before I came in. Not at night, though. And I’ve barely eaten all weekend—last thing was a small chicken sandwich.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. You also mentioned feeling lightheaded when standing. Is that new or something you’ve had before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s been going on for a while. I’ve had it since my transplant. Sometimes my heart races too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, we’ll check your blood pressure sitting and standing. We’ll also monitor your heart rate. We’re going to run some tests to figure out what’s causing the nausea and slow digestion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it my stomach not emptying? I’ve felt like food just sits there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a possibility. Given your history of diabetes from steroids and your medications, we’re concerned about gastroparesis. We’ll schedule a gastric emptying study to check that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on Reglan before. It helped, but I stopped because of the diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We may restart it at a lower dose. We’ll watch closely. For now, let’s start with clear liquids and see how you tolerate them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs show your liver enzymes are elevated—ALT and AST are high. We’re concerned this could be related to your GVHD. We’d like to do a liver biopsy to check.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A biopsy? Is that safe? I’ve never had one before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s safe. It’s done with ultrasound guidance, and you’ll get light sedation. The goal is to see if your liver is affected by GVHD, so we can adjust your prednisone dose safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, if it helps us figure things out, I’ll do it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The liver biopsy was done this morning. Two samples were taken, no complications. We’ll get results in a few days. How’s your stomach today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still full feeling. I tried soup last night and didn’t finish it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you on IV fluids for now. The gastric emptying study is scheduled for tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The gastric emptying study is back. It shows 85% of food still in your stomach after four hours. That’s severely delayed. You have gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s why I feel so full. Can we treat it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re restarting metoclopramide—Reglan—at 5 mg four times a day. Lower than before to avoid worsening diarrhea. We’re also stopping the senna and docusate—they can make diarrhea worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ve been using them since I was constipated, but maybe I don’t need them now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your endoscopy was normal—no ulcers or blockages. That’s good. But we still need to understand the diarrhea. You finally had a bowel movement, so we sent a stool sample.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could it be an infection? I haven’t been around sick people.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’re checking for bacteria, parasites, and C. diff. Your CMV test came back negative, so it’s not that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re still waiting on the stool culture. Your heart rate has been high—up to 130. You’re not feverish, and your EKG is normal except for sinus tachycardia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s been doing that for years. I get lightheaded, and my heart races. Is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not immediately. Cardiology thinks it could be due to dehydration or autonomic issues. You responded well to a liter of IV fluids—your heart rate dropped to 90. We’ll keep encouraging you to drink.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Big update: your stool culture is positive for Campylobacter, a bacterial infection. It’s treatable with antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Campylobacter? How did I get that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Usually from undercooked poultry or contaminated water. We don’t always find the source. We’re starting azithromycin—two doses in the hospital, then seven more at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that stop the diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should help. We’ll also keep you on the lower-dose Reglan for gastroparesis. Your nausea should improve as your stomach starts moving food along.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver biopsy results are in. No signs of liver GVHD. That’s excellent news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that means I can reduce my prednisone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re reducing it from 17.5 mg to 15 mg daily. This lowers your risk of infections, bone loss, and other steroid side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I’ve had so many fractures already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Your diarrhea has improved, and you’re tolerating soft foods. Your heart rate is stable in the 90s.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. I even had a small piece of toast this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great progress. Neurology saw you for the lightheadedness and tachycardia. They don’t think it’s autonomic instability, but we’re checking thiamine and some antibodies just to be sure. Results are pending.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Should I worry about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not at all. It’s just being thorough. The main issues—gastroparesis and infection—are under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge tomorrow. Your labs are stable, you’re eating well, and your symptoms have improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take your Reglan 5 mg four times a day—before meals and at bedtime. Finish the azithromycin for seven days. Drink plenty of fluids to avoid dehydration and keep your heart rate down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the prednisone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay on 15 mg daily. Your outpatient team will guide any further taper. Keep using your eye drops for GVHD—Mass Eye & Ear wants you on those every two hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been doing that. They help with the dryness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Continue your insulin as before—NPH 10 units in the morning. Your blood sugar was well-controlled here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the enoxaparin for blood clots?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue daily. You’re on lifelong anticoagulation due to your history of DVTs and PE.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your primary team in a week. GI wants to follow up on the gastroparesis. And we’ll get those pending antibody tests back—someone will call if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I think I understand. Take Reglan, finish the antibiotic, stay on prednisone and insulin, and drink fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And call if you have severe nausea, vomiting, or dizziness that doesn’t improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. Your discharge summary is ready, and a nurse will go over your medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel so much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well. Remember: the azithromycin is important—finish all doses. And keep taking the Reglan even if you feel fine—it helps your stomach empty.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll make sure to drink more water during the day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m just glad to be going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad you’re feeling better. Don’t hesitate to call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep that in mind. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will be in shortly to assist with discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to help. Take it easy at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe journey.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll be in touch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.
